Muscle Contraction. The coordinated shortening of muscle fibers, powered by ATP hydrolysis and driven by the sliding of thick filaments, which are myosin, past thin filaments, which are actin. Initiated by nerve signals that trigger calcium release, contraction requires precise orchestration of motor proteins, ion pumps, and contractile machinery. This fundamental process enables movement, posture, and the mechanical work that defines animal physiology.

The sliding filament model describes contraction. Myosin heads, or cross-bridges, bind actin and pull the thin filament in a power stroke fueled by ATP hydrolysis, then release and reset for the next cycle. Rigor mortis occurs when ATP production ceases. Without ATP, myosin cannot release from actin, locking muscles in contraction. Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind troponin, shifting tropomyosin on actin to expose myosin-binding sites.

Sodium influx depolarizes the muscle cell membrane. This electrical signal spreads along the sarcolemma and down T-tubules, triggering calcium release. Potassium efflux repolarizes the muscle cell after contraction, restoring the resting membrane potential and enabling the next contraction. Motor units—a single motor neuron and all muscle fibers it innervates—are the functional units of contraction, recruited in order of size. Small units fire first, large units only for forceful movements.

ATP provides two critical functions. It energizes the myosin power stroke, and it provides the energy to break the myosin-actin cross-bridge, essential for relaxation. Z-disks mark the boundaries of sarcomeres and anchor thin filaments. The distance between Z-disks decreases during contraction as thin filaments slide past thick filaments.

Muscle fatigue results from depletion of creatine phosphate stores, lactate accumulation, and calcium handling dysfunction. These factors diminish force production over time. Muscle fiber types differ: Type I slow-twitch fibers are suited to endurance, while Type II fast-twitch fibers produce power, differentiated by myosin isoforms and metabolic capacity.
